claims.text: Mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiTi powder has elemental segregation.
Mechanical alloying gives the CoCrFeNiTi powder high surface energy.
High-energy ball milling induces severe plastic deformation and elemental mixing.
Rapid sintering kinetically traps a high-temperature FCC phase in CoCrFeNiTi.
A sintering temperature of 900–1000 °C lies just below the HCP nucleation threshold for CoCrFeNiTi.
A heating rate below 50 °C/min manages thermal-expansion mismatch during sintering.
A dwell time below 10 minutes prevents HCP nucleation.
Applying 50–100 MPa during SPS suppresses porosity.
A grain size below 100 nm kinetically inhibits the FCC-to-HCP transformation.
A high density of stacking faults and twins helps kinetically stabilize metastable FCC against HCP transformation.
Suppressing ZrHf-rich segregation prevents HCP nucleation in the proposed CoCrFeNiTi alloy.
Slow cooling associated with HIP can produce a secondary ZrHf-rich HCP phase in Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20.
The proposed rapid-sintering rate exceeds a critical rate needed to avoid diffusion-controlled HCP formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanocrystallinity increases the nucleation barrier for HCP and thereby favors metastable FCC.
The proposed process will produce CoCrFeNiTi with less than 1% porosity.
The processed alloy will have a dominant nanocrystalline FCC phase with a minor BCC phase and no significant HCP phase.
Grain refinement will significantly increase hardness relative to cast CoCrFeNiTi.
Solid-solution strengthening will also contribute to the hardness increase.
Formation of an HCP phase is associated with increased brittleness.
Varying nanoindentation loads from 0.1 to 10 mN and dwell times from 1 to 100 s can separate grain-boundary strengthening from solute strengthening.

contradictions.description: The target alloy contains Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti but no Zr or Hf, yet the proposed mediator and boundary conditions invoke suppression of a ZrHf-rich segregated phase.

The mechanism requires a rapid heating rate exceeding an unspecified critical minimum, whereas the only quantitative heating-rate condition is an upper limit below 50 °C/min; this does not establish that the process is rapid enough.

The boundary suggests HCP stability or rapid HCP nucleation at temperatures above about 1100 °C, but the experiment describes 1050 °C as above the predicted safe window and as a condition intended to promote HCP.
